articles.title: Democrats win House by largest margin in 50 years. And, COP31 ends with no deal
articles.summary: Democrats have currently flipped 47 House seats and could flip 49 total. And, climate change talks at COP31 ran two days longer than expected, becoming the longest conference in the summit's history.
body: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Vote counts are concluding for the 2026 midterm elections, revealing a better picture of just how much Democrats dominated. Fifty-six percent of voters chose the Democrats in House races compared to 42% for Republicans. The 14-point gap is the largest margin won by Democrats in 50 years. The party has officially won the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s. Take a look at NPR's breakdown of the U.S. House races, by the numbers.

Artificial intelligence is causing significant swings in the stock market as investors speculate about the future of the technology boom. While AI stocks have driven markets to record highs and bolstered the economy, concerns are growing about a potential bubble. Investors anticipated that AI giant Anthropic's stock market debut last week would lift markets, but instead Wall Street experienced one of its worst weeks in recent times.

Poland has called an emergency NATO session for today after Russia fired three cruise missiles into its territory. The incident highlights the stakes for European countries in Russia's war on Ukraine, prompting nations along NATO's eastern border to seek enhanced air defense support. Poland plans to present proposals to increase surveillance capabilities and deploy more F-35s to intercept incoming missiles and drones.

Delegates at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, couldn't agree on a plan over the weekend to address fossil fuels, the main cause of climate change. The event ran two days longer than expected, making it the longest in the history of these summits. Nearly 200 nations failed to finalize targets for electrification and financial aid for developing countries, or to address the impacts of climate change. The European Union rejected any conclusion that didn't advocate for a transition away from fossil fuels, while oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed this position. Fossil fuels contribute about 73% of global emissions.

NPR's annual reading guide, Books We Love, is back with more than 380 new recommendations from staff and trusted critics. This year's picks span a range of genres, including fiction, cookbooks, children's reads, poetry and science fiction. Don't worry if it looks overwhelming; the interactive filters will help you narrow down your list and find your next great read. And why stop at this year's reads? The Books We Love archive has 14 years of recommendations, so you can discover more than 4,700 amazing books, all in one place. This year's edition of Books We Love is dedicated to Rose Friedman, who edited a dozen editions and worked at NPR for 15 years before her death this year at age 38. Friedman was one of the original founders of Books We Love, formerly known as The Book Concierge. In her honor, start exploring and find something wonderful to read today.
by Maria Godoy, senior science and health editor and correspondent

People had warned me it might be tough to get Amish people to talk to me as a journalist — and probably impossible to get their permission to record their voice. Not a great omen for compelling radio storytelling.

Yet as I headed off to Lancaster County, Pa., last month to report on the biggest and deadliest measles outbreak in the U.S. in decades, I knew I wanted to hear directly from the community hit hardest.

So I turned to some good old shoe-leather reporting. My producer and I mapped out Amish-owned businesses in and around Lancaster County and spent a day driving around from shop to shop. At every stop, we introduced ourselves and explained the focus of our story. We asked Amish people (easily identifiable by their traditional dress) about their views on the measles outbreak and vaccination. While some declined to talk, others opened up about how measles had affected their families and communities, and why they had or hadn't decided to get vaccinated. To my surprise, one woman even let me record her voice.

Outside a farm supply store in a rural town, I met an Amish woman who was visibly pregnant. Measles can have devastating consequences during pregnancy. She told me her husband and two children had gotten vaccinated to protect her and her unborn child. She declined to give me her name at first, then got in a car driven by her hired non-Amish driver. As they exited the parking lot, the driver stopped to ask us what media outlet we were with. "Oh, NPR!" the driver said when we replied. Then she turned to her Amish passenger and told her, "Don't worry, you can trust them."

Part of gaining trust is about showing up, showing respect and really listening. Word gets around that you're trustworthy. Public health officials in Pennsylvania have also been using a similar approach to win the trust of Amish people as they seek to boost vaccination rates in the current outbreak. You can read more about it here.
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones hit a Russian warship at a naval base in Libya, Zelenskyy says
articles.summary: Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, claiming that sea drones sank the navy vessel in a surprise assault.
body: KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, claiming that sea drones sank the navy vessel in a surprise assault the previous day.

Ukrainian forces deployed seven domestically made sea drones in the operation, which struck the Russian navy corvette in the Mediterranean, according to Zelenskyy. The ship was one of Russia's newest vessels, commissioned a year after Moscow launched the 2022 invasion of its neighbor, the Ukrainian leader said in a post on X.
Russian officials made no immediate comment.
The operation, conducted some 2,400 kilometers (1,500 miles) from the front line in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv's forces.

Ukraine has at times blindsided Russia during the war with ingenious attacks that embarrass Moscow, such as Operation Spiderweb in June last year, when drones launched from trucks hit over 40 aircraft parked near air bases across Russia. Along the roughly 1,250-kilometer (almost 800-mile) front line snaking through eastern and southern Ukraine, Kyiv's cutting-edge drones and ground robots are helping hold back Russia's bigger army.
At the same time, Russia's strategic bombing of Ukraine has devastated the power grid ahead of winter and damaged civilian buildings.

A Russian strike on a five-story apartment block in a village near Kyiv killed 11 people, regional police said Monday. A 7-year-old child and a 79-year-old woman were pulled from the rubble after the Sunday morning attack, rescue services said.
Zelenskyy described Sunday's attack as "exemplary" and said "the targets we set were achieved."
"We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons," he said.

Ukraine has hit Russian oil refineries as far away as western Siberia and Russian warships in the Mediterranean, Zelenskyy noted in a live video address Monday to a meeting of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.
"We keep finding ways to get back on our feet after every Russian attack," Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian forces also struck the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said Moscow used to transport weapons, and destroyed a Ka-27 military helicopter in the attack, the Ukrainian leader said.

Ukrainian forces are operating in western Libya under a covert deal endorsed by the West, using the North African country's territory to strike a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in March, according to Libyan officials.

The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, were at the time operating mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also in other military facilities in the capital Tripoli and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press earlier this year.
Sunday's attack severely damaged the Russian corvette at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya, according to two Libyan officials.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the base early Sunday. Civil defense units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The vessel had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, a statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

The government in eastern Libya sent a letter to U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres and the U.N. Security Council, calling for an international investigation into the potential use of western Libya to prepare and launch Sunday's attack.

Libyan officials who were briefed on the attack told The Associated Press that at least four drones were intercepted while two hit the corvette, which is designed to patrol coastal waters and escort other ships.
At least 10 people, including Libyan and Russian nationals, were wounded in the attack, one of the officials said.
The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.

Ambrey, a U.K.-based maritime security and risk intelligence firm, said that some of the explosions at the Benghazi Naval Base were likely caused by the detonation of ammunition on board the Russian warship.
Hours after the warship attack, another sea drone strike hit a Maltese-flagged commercial vessel sailing off Benghazi, the Libyan coast guard said.

Ukraine's Security Service, or SBU, described the operation as "unique." It said the cargo ship MV Angara was sanctioned and used to transport Russian military equipment, and the multipurpose corvette Merkury regularly escorted Russian naval convoys, including guarding the MV Angara.
The drones were delivered to a designated location and launched from a so-called "mothership" near the target, the SBU said.
A Ka-27 helicopter was on board the corvette and also went under, the SBU added.
Russian defenses tried from air, sea and land to hit the attacking drones, it said.
"Ukraine's defense forces have once again shown that the Russian navy and its logistics have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea," which borders both Russia and Ukraine, the SBU said.

articles.title: Lebanese villagers return to wrecked homes as the Israeli army pulls back
articles.summary: In a pilot project in a village in southern Lebanon, Israeli forces have left and the Lebanese army moved it. But villagers who return find their houses wrecked.
body: ZAWTAR AL-GHARBIYAH, Lebanon — After two decades of working installing vehicle air conditioning in Saudi Arabia, Atef Kadouh saved up enough money to build a house in his hometown in southern Lebanon.
He and his wife, Soumaya Yaghi lived in the house for 40 years and had five children — all born at home.
A photo of the youngest, Adel, is propped up in a basket of dried flowers near the doorway.

Adel, clean-cut with a trimmed beard, was a sports teacher and a basketball champion who was planning to travel to France this summer to pursue his doctorate. When the war with Israel began this year, he decided to volunteer as an ambulance driver.
The Israeli military killed him and four other medics on March 28 in a drone strike as the first responders buried a 75-year-old man who had died in hospital.

"This one broke me," his father says. "He was my youngest son, 27 years old. There have been wars in every country in the world but there are rules for war … you attack a paramedic rescuing wounded people, children? He was not a fighter at the front."
He says he warned his son that Israel could not be trusted not to kill medical personnel.
"He would not listen to me. He said, 'Dad there are wounded children — we have to go rescue them,'" he says.
Lebanon's Health Ministry says Israel has killed more than 135 first responders and medical staff in the past two years.

Asked about this airstrike, the Israeli military replied, without providing proof, that militants routinely pose as paramedics and transport weapons in ambulances for the militant group Hezbollah and its allies.
It did not respond to follow-up questions pointing out the five were not killed in an ambulance but at a burial.
The Kadouh family returned to the village in July when it became the first and until now only test of a U.S.-brokered plan for Israeli forces to withdraw and the Lebanese army to take over.

The plan is aimed at keeping Iran-backed Hezbollah out of the area, after they started firing rockets across the nearby border in solidarity with the Palestinian militant group Hamas who launched a surprise attack on southern Israel in October 2023.

Israel responded with devastating air strikes and eventually a ground invasion, and says it has continued attacks in south Lebanon following a U.S.-brokered ceasefire this year to eliminate what it believes are continued threats to northern Israel. Israel's defense minister has acknowledged destroying more than 20,000 homes across the Lebanese border in a self-declared security zone.
When Kadouh and Yaghi returned to the village, they found that Israeli soldiers had occupied their house. And then it had been set on fire.
Upstairs in the hallway, near scorched walls and shattered windows, what appeared to be a work roster was written on the wall in blue marker in Hebrew with the first names of Israeli soldiers.

Almost everything in the house had been destroyed. Appliances — the fridge, freezer and washing machine — had bullet holes in them. Some, along with furniture, had been pushed over the second floor balcony, smashing on the ground below.
Kadouh says they knew from satellite photos there was destruction in their village "but the level of destruction — we were not expecting that. Everything that could be broken they broke."
In the kitchen were shattered floor tiles and kitchen cupboards wrenched from the walls.
The fire appeared to be set as the soldiers were leaving. Blackened, burned food packets — fruit boxes and cans of energy drinks with Hebrew writing — were on the floor along with rotting sandwiches.
In their 18-month-old grandson's bedroom, soot from a scorched ceiling dripped down on walls decorated with images of hot-air balloons and teddy bears climbing ladders to the moon.

Yaghi shows a bullet — one of many she says she found throughout the house. The spent engine casing of a missile or a drone with English markings reading "propulsion unit – tactical" was found in one of the rooms.
There is no running water or electricity — Kadouh says the Israeli military destroyed the solar panels.
The Lebanese army told them that when it reentered the village many of the houses had been rigged to be blown up. It said it dismantled explosives left by Israeli forces in their house and others.
The Israeli army did not reply to NPR queries about why the house was damaged or set on fire. It said military policy bars burning homes or leaving explosives.
Unable to enter the village while Israeli forces were there, Kadouh said he saw a tank in their courtyard from drone images posted on social media.

Yaghi says the Israeli army used a bulldozer to uproot the trees — including the pine trees which yield one of their most prized cash crops: pine nuts. When they had killed the trees, she says they demolished the family's garage and destroyed their tractor.
"We are back to square one," Kadouh says. "Starting from scratch."
Even more precarious, though, than when they started decades ago. Despite a ceasefire, smoke rises from a nearby village where Israel is still attacking.
Amid all the damage, the destruction of the family's trees cuts the deepest.
"I tended to them as if they were small children — they were all dear to me," Kadouh says.
Yaghi points out where there were fruit-bearing cactus, olive trees, a fig tree one of her sons brought from Italy, avocado trees and fields of thyme, avocado.
Up until a decade ago, almost everyone here grew tobacco, diversifying crops when that market collapsed.
"We raised our children through hard work and thank God all of them were educated," Yaghi says, noting with pride that they all became professionals.
She maintains a visceral connection to the land.

"Record this," she asks, walking next to rose bushes that have begun to bloom again. "Our land is a paradise with everything in it. Our life is this land. Our life is our homes. Even if we were to die in our homes it would be much better than to live outside."
Villagers here feel abandoned by even their own government — and still in danger from nearby Israeli forces.

"Our homes were destroyed and no one came to check on us," Kadouh says. "Not the Lebanese state or outsiders or the parties," he says, referring to Hezbollah and its allies. "They just say 'Go back, go back' to the village. We came back and there are no essentials — no electricity, no water."

Kadouh has a son in the Lebanese army and another in national security services but he says, because the Lebanese army is deliberately underequipped to avoid presenting a threat to Israel, they have never been allowed to do their jobs.

"The Lebanese state never sent a soldier here to protect us," he says." That is why the parties and others came in — Hezbollah or Amal or even the Palestinian factions decades ago. "But the vacuum that the Lebanese state has left brought us to this tragedy" he says.
"We love the Lebanese army — let them bring us an army, but let them protect us," he says. "This army has a rifle — Israel has an F-35" fighter jet.
"But we would rather sit in the dirt," he says. "Our soul, our life is here, I was born here."
Kadouh says maybe someday there will be peace with Israel, but after all the deaths and destruction, not in his lifetime — and not with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"Netanyahu is the one who killed my son. Let him bring back my son," he says. "If just yesterday Israel killed my son, am I supposed to tell the Israelis, 'Put your hand in my hand'? If they want to be our neighbors they should do good. Instead they burn us."

articles.title: Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuels
articles.summary: Some 200 countries gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the annual climate negotiations. Countries failed to reach an agreement over fossil fuels - the primary driver of global warming.
body: ANTALYA, Turkey – International climate change talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours over the main cause of planetary warming — fossil fuels. On Sunday, nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from energy sources like coal and natural gas.

The talks ended in a dramatic fashion, with the European Union negotiators saying they could not agree to a final agreement without mentioning the transition away from fossil fuels — the primary driver of climate change. The EU bloc then walked out of the room. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal make up roughly 73% of global emissions.
After representatives of the EU walked out, other countries also objected – including Panama and island states such as the Marshall Islands.

The European climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, said that when the world is heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."

This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been scientific consensus that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.

Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts, like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035. That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.

"It's good that that decision has been rejected," says Mohamed Adow, of Power Shift Africa, a nonprofit focused on climate change in Africa. "It doesn't have enough to help protect the people who are most vulnerable to climate change, who have contributed the least and are now suffering firsthand the worst."
NPR correspondent Michael Copley contributed to this story. This story was edited by Sadie Babits.

articles.title: Mexico detains top cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro,' setting off violence
articles.summary: Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, better known as "El Chapo Isidro," was one of the FBI's most wanted fugitives. His arrest in northwest Mexico on Saturday has sparked violence in the region.
body: MEXICO CITY — Gunfire rang out, trucks burned and Mexican forces clashed with cartel gunmen in the state of Sinaloa overnight as Mexican authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro."

Meza Flores was one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives and a top cartel leader from the Beltrán Leyva criminal organization wanted for trafficking drugs to the United States and illegally carrying firearms.

Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores.

He was also a key ally to "Los Mayos," a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.
Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups.
But experts warn that it could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions.

Mexican authorities said they used "stealth and surprise" to capture Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him. He was later taken by aircraft to Mexico City to appear before prosecutors.

Video shared by authorities shows heavily armed men in camouflage escorting a man through a dimly lit house and putting him in the back of a truck. No casualties have been reported so far as a result of the operation.
The capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence overnight with calm setting in Saturday morning.

Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders.

As a result, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to discuss the case.

"Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary," the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least "10 roadblocks" with burning vehicles on Guasave's streets.
Guasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations.
"Last night, many businesses were burned ... along with cars and trucks," Sánchez told The Associated Press.

She said that the city's firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning.
"Everything looks calm today," Sánchez said.
Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians.

Meza Flores' detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.
The U.S. and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the DEA commending Mexican authorities.

"The capture of El Chapo Isidro delivers a significant blow to a ruthless criminal organization that has used extreme violence to traffic deadly drugs, including fentanyl, a designated weapon of mass destruction, into American communities," the DEA said in a statement. "This operation underscores the critical importance of intelligence sharing in targeting dangerous cartel leaders."
García Harfuch called the detention "an important step in pacifying Sinaloa."

Sheinbaum's government has targeted a number of cartel kingpins, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as " El Mencho," who was killed by the military in February.

Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said that the capture of Meza Flores marked another case of the governments of Mexico and the U.S. increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy, which critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run.

The so-called kingpin strategy relies on zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores as a way to combat cartels. But experts say that it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa.

"What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States," Saucedo said. "What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don't dismantle the entire organization. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact."

articles.title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
articles.summary: Libya's eastern government says the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia.
body: Satellite imagery showed a ship on fire at the port early on Sunday morning
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.
It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.

Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.

Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.

GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.

articles.title: COP31 fails to reach major climate deal as talks expose deep divisions
articles.summary: The talks fail to make a breakthrough on tackling climate change after a row about mentioning fossil fuels.
body: Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.
Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.
But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.
The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.
UN secretary general Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".
After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday morning to try to break the deadlock.

But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".
"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.
Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.
A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.
Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.
Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".
What’s next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?
Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.
Last year at COP30 in Brazil, nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.
But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.
"Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.
The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing".

"This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".
While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.
Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said that there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.
He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.
The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal.
And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.

In the Paris talks of 2015, nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change.
The UN says that the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century.
Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says.
But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.

Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.
The COP31 president also said that more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035
But following today's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.
The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia.
"[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work," but acknowledged it "fell short" today.
The UN climate process has "suffered setback before and come back stronger," Stiell told delegates. "It must do so again."

articles.title: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
articles.summary: The report says there are signs of possible contamination across almost all of Gaza as a result of Israel's actions.
body: The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza in almost two years (file photo)

Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the non-profit organisation Oxfam says, external.

Heavy metals, explosive residues, and asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins and biological contaminants in the air, soil and water supply are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.
Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, accuses Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza."
"The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival," he says.
Israel's government has been asked for its response to the report.

It has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. Israel maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.
The report says 99% of Gaza shows indicators of potential environmental contamination

Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.

The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".

Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.
"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.
She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.
Only a small fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes of debris in Gaza has been cleared

With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.

Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.
UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.

The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.
Recent winter storms caused rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent camps

Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.

A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.
"There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."
Dr Alaa Abu Hajar has seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war
Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.

"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.

Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

articles.title: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
articles.summary: Nine people are dead in the attack, with rescue efforts ongoing to find those still missing from the residential building.
body: 'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes hit Kyiv

A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer after 14 hours, in overnight Russian strikes on Dymer, in the Kyiv region, that killed nine people, Ukrainian officials have said.
The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.
A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday.
Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life.
Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.
Response teams including police, explosive technicians, dog handlers and medics are continuing with rescue efforts.
In a telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.
Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.
The attack on the residential building occurred in the early hours of the morning while people were asleep
Zelensky said more than 130 people are involved in emergency operations at the scene, and that they will continue until they have "complete information about every single person".
Sending his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed, he said the strike struck the residential building, "practically blowing a section of it to smithereens".
Zelensky added that "rescue efforts are complicated by constant new air raid alerts and renewed threats".
The strike hit the building at 05:00 local time, when families were still asleep, Ukraine's minister of internal affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said.
More than 70 strikes have been launched across 10 Ukrainian regions as of Sunday evening, Vyhivskyi added.
Emergency workers continue to search for those missing after Russian drone and missile attacks in Dymer.
In his video address posted online, Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 injured in a strike on an "ordinary grocery store" in Vyshneve.
Tkachenko previously said two other people were killed and eight wounded in the Vyshneve attack.
Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine's Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said in a post on X., external

articles.title: Flights and train services cancelled in Belgium due to strike
articles.summary: A series of strikes have hit Belgium in recent months as the prime minister struggles to agree a budget to cut costs.
body: A few people have turned up at Brussels airport where no flights are leaving
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem as well as at Charleroi, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Underground services have also been halted in capital Brussels, where large numbers of people joined a protest march.

The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.
No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers.
"In total, 404 flights today cannot be operated, which has an impact on more than 50,000 passengers," Brussels Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens said.

Reuters news agency spoke to Florence Faure, a French passenger who had arrived in Brussels from China's capital, Beijing, only to find that her flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport had been cancelled.
"Since our luggage was supposed to go on to Paris Charles de Gaulle, we didn't even collect it," she said.
A similar situation has affected Charleroi, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure or arrival.
One passenger told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that she had received no warning and only discovered there were no flights when she arrived at the airport.
Philippe Naime, a teacher, was one of the tens of thousands taking part in the protest march in Brussels.
"Quite simply, no more money is being invested in education, and people are left to fend for themselves. But people do not have the means to do that," he told Reuters.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.
Large numbers of people have descended on Brussels for a protest march
The Belgian prime minister leads a five-party coalition.

One of its members, the socialist Vooruit, has been refusing to endorse plans agreed by the other four. It wants to raise taxes on the rich and for there to be fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
De Wever met King Philippe on Monday for the third update since the impasse.

"While expressing regret over the lack of significant progress, the king encouraged the prime minister to persevere in order to reach an agreement as soon as possible," the royal palace said in a statement.
The leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
Bert Engelaar, head of the union, called for "a genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes".
"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," he added, praising the Vooruit party.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

articles.title: Mexican soldiers attacked in wake of drug lord's arrest
articles.summary: Eight suspects are arrested after firing on soldiers trying to re-establish order following the arrest of 'El Chapo Isidro'.
body: Extra forces have been deployed to guard the facility where 'Chapo Isidro' is in custody
Mexican soldiers have detained eight alleged members of a drug cartel whose leader was arrested on Friday, sparking a wave of violence in northern Sinaloa state.

The Mexican defence ministry said the soldiers were shot by the suspects on Sunday while on patrol in the town of Sinaloa de Leyva, trying to re-establish order in the wake of the arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.
Meza Flores, also known as "Chapo Isidro", was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list and had managed to evade capture for years.
The ministry said the eight had also been involved in the retaliatory violence unleashed by Meza Flores's cartel in the hours after his arrest on Friday.
In a statement published on social media, external, the ministry of defence said that one of the detainees was under age.
It added that its special forces had seized six vehicles as part of their operation, two of which had been fitted with bullet-proof armour and gun turrets.
The US Department of Justice described Friday's arrest of Meza Flores as "a spectacular military operation" and congratulated Mexico's military and special forces on his capture.
It said that the US Homeland Security Task Force had supported the Mexican military and praised the "bilateral effort".
Watch: Suspected drug lord 'El Chapo Isidro' transferred to Mexico's capital
Mexico's defence ministry said its special forces had used stealth and surprise to reach the home of the wanted man.
They also established a security perimeter to prevent Meza Flores from escaping and cartel reinforcements from arriving.
Nevertheless, a bloody firefight ensued.
Along with Meza Flores, his second-in-command, known as "Serafín", and his financial operator, were also arrested and quickly transferred by air to Mexico City.
As news of their arrest spread, members of their cartel erected barricades on major roads and set cars and some shops alight.
There were also reports of shoot-outs between the security forces and cartel members.
The prosecutor's office in Sinaloa says 17 people, four of them members of the Mexican security forces, were killed as a result of the violence on Friday and early Saturday.
US Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva has described Meza Flores as "the most dangerous man in Mexico".
"For decades Meza Flores has promoted the terrorist objectives of the Sinaloa cartel," Duva said, accusing him of "flooding the United States with deadly substances".
The 44-year-old is believed to have started his criminal career with the Juárez cartel decades ago.
He later moved on to become the right-hand man of the leader of the Beltrán Leyva Organisation, a drug gang once allied to the Sinaloa cartel before the two groups split and became bitter enemies.
As early as 2013, the US Treasury identified Meza Flores as the leader of his own drug-trafficking organisation, named after him.

The US Treasury said at the time, that the Meza Flores drug trafficking organisation was responsible for "the distribution of large quantities of methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and cocaine to the United States".
It added that the turf war between the Meza Flores cartel and the Sinaloa cartel had "resulted in the quadrupling of drug-war killings" in between 2009 and 2013.
According to think tank Insight Crime, external, Meza Flores himself kept a low profile over the last decade while continuing to run his cartel out of Guasave, in Sinaloa state.

The head of the US Drug Enforcement Administration said that his capture was a "significant blow to a ruthless criminal organisation that has used extreme violence to traffic deadly drugs, including fentanyl, a designated weapon of mass destruction, into American communities".
His arrest, and the co-operation between US and Mexican officials which led to it, will be seen as a win for the government of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum.
Sheinbaum has stressed that she is keen to work with the US authorities to capture high-profile target as long as Mexican's sovereignty is respected.

articles.title: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony
articles.summary: The couple have been together for four years and were engaged in 2025.
body: Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.
A string of black and white photos shared by the Flowers singer on Instagram showed the pair kissing while surrounded by white roses.

Her mother, Trisha Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, could be seen in the background of one image. Her father Billy Ray Cyrus was not in the picture but was at the ceremony with his partner, actress Liz Hurley.
Grammy-winning Cyrus, 33, wore a white silk dress designed by Anthony Vaccarello for Saint Laurent, while 28-year-old drummer Morando said "I do" in a black suit from the same fashion house.
In one of the photographs, which was the first in a series of images shared by the singer in an Instagram post, the newly weds posed next to a golden retriever.
The post was captioned with "M+M" followed by a white heart and the ceremony date, 21 November.
Miley's sister Brandi Cyrus, singer Doechii and fashion designer Donatella Versace were among those to congratulate the couple in the comments.
The ceremony reportedly took place at a resort formerly owned by Fly Me To The Moon singer Frank Sinatra.
Guests stuck to an all-black dress code, according to reports.
'Angel by my side' - Miley Cyrus pays tribute to godmother Dolly Parton
Miley Cyrus confirms engagement to musician Maxx Morando
The American singer confirmed her engagement to the 28-year-old drummer during an interview with US TV show Good Morning America last year.
She said Morando had got down on one knee for the proposal during a trip to Asia.
"I am not easy to surprise because I love to control every situation and I had completely surrendered and I'm telling you, I was so, so, so surprised," she said.
During an interview with Wonderland, Morando said he "had to be really sneaky" to keep his proposal plans a secret.

"We went to Tokyo first for a couple days, and then on to Kyoto. I think she had a sense that it was coming, so I was waiting until the very last moment of the very last day to throw her off the scent as much as I could," he said.
Cyrus, 33, had previously been married to Australian actor Liam Hemsworth but the couple separated in 2019.
The singer, whose hits include Party in the U.S.A and Wrecking Ball, married Hunger Games star Hemsworth in 2018 after the couple were in a relationship for a decade.
Speaking to British Vogue in 2023, Cyrus said she and 28-year-old Morando met after being "put on a blind date".

Morando is a drummer with LA-based band Liily. The band participated in NBC's Miley's New Year's Eve Party - hosted by Cyrus - in 2022, alongside musicians including Cyrus's late godmother Dolly Parton and David Byrne.

articles.title: Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict
articles.summary: The two leaders committed to upholding sovereignty and "non-interference in the internal affairs of states".
body: The meeting between Kenya's President William Ruto (left) and DR Congo's Félix Tshisekedi (centre) was hosted by Denis Sassou Nguesso (right)

Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.
This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.
On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".

The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé as mediator.
Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".
DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).

DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.
DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.
When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.

The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.
DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.
Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader
Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila, in October 2025.
Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.
He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.
Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.
The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.

On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.
Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.
More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.
The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.

articles.title: Presidential villa suffers water and power cuts, Nigerian leader says
articles.summary: Bola Tinubu says he was shaving last week when the water cut out - an experience familiar to many Nigerians.
body: Bola Tinubu promised to address the country's electricity problems while campaigning for the 2023 election
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - issues that are all too common for the country's ordinary citizens.
He said he was shaving last week when the water supply cut at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja.
He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues.
Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.
He explained: "On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won't know punishment dey dia too [there’s punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].
"The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,” he said.
Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.
Can Nigeria's president regain voters' trust after painful first term?
Search and rescue teams race against time after Nigeria boat tragedy

Nigeria has long endured electricity shortages, but recent severe disruptions have been caused primarily by insufficient gas supplies and declining hydropower output, rather than the usual nationwide grid collapse.
Persistent blackouts in Lagos, Abuja and elsewhere have forced distribution companies to implement rotating power cuts, severely impacting households and businesses.

The country also suffers from chronic water shortages, the result of a structural crisis rooted in the gap between rapid urban population growth and decaying, inadequate public water infrastructure, leaving millions without reliable supplies, especially in Lagos.
Many Nigerians rely on generators like these to power their homes and businesses

Tinubu made a high-profile electricity promise during the 2023 election campaign, but the exact wording and how binding it is has become a major point of contention ahead of the election on 16 January 2027.

In 2022, months before the last presidential election, Tinubu said: "Whichever way, by all means necessary, you will have electricity, and you will not pay for estimated bills any more. A promise made will be a promise kept.
"If I don't keep the promise and I come for a second term, don't vote for me, unless I give you adequate reasons why I couldn't deliver,” he said.

Despite the continuing power cuts, some of his supporters point to improved electricity supplies in rural areas as well as a recently approved $2bn (£1.5bn) investment in a new East–West Super Grid, designed to expand electricity transmission capacity and strengthen the national grid, as evidence that he is doing his best to keep to his promise.
Tinubu defeated the country’s former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as well as former Anambra state governor Peter Obi in 2023 and the three are seen as the strongest contenders once again.

articles.title: Russia-bound ship attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.summary: Finnish defence forces say that Ukraine was likely behind the drone attack on the vessel.
body: The Finnish Border Guard is leading the operations involving the Sparta II
A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.

The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."

The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.

The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

articles.title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
articles.summary: Choi Kyo-jin admits last-minute measures to stop AI-assisted cheating during the college entrance exam caused chaos.
body: How South Korea tackles cheating on its college entrance exam
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.
He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.

A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.
The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.
South Korean high school pupils in Daegu check their answers, a day after the annual college entrance exam
"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.
This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.
This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

articles.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
articles.summary: Democrats have now won at least 258 seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats.
body: Chuck Hubbard is a former journalist whose first political campaign was in 2022
The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.
The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.
The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.
Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.
View the 2026 midterm election results

Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

She conceded on Sunday, saying in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."
Virginia Foxx spent a decade in the North Carolina Senate before representing the state in the House of Representatives
Hubbard, meanwhile, wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

He added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.
Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.
President Donald Trump himself - as well as Vice President JD Vance - have suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses.
Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.

The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.

Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.
However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

articles.title: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
articles.summary: The Army says "swift action" is necessary to protect its personnel and nearby communities around its ammunition plant in Iowa.
body: The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.

"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."
The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.
The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.

In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.

"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.
It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".
The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.

Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place.

Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.
On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible.
Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.

The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".

One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen.
"There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement.
The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, which filed the lawsuit on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause, filed a new motion on Sunday in response to the army's filing.
The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.

The motion includes declarations from environmental experts and local officials who support pausing the detonation, citing a lack of public notice and questioning the Army's claim that delay would cause significant risks.
