articles.title: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
articles.summary: At least three people were killed and 36 are still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory.
body: At least three people have been killed and 36 are still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory in western Java on Saturday.
Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for the missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.
Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.
The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.
Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening.

Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.
"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.
Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.

Firefighters had been called to the building at 16:30 local time (09:30 GMT) on Saturday - but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.
"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.
The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.
On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

articles.title: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
articles.summary: Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores, who is accused of drug trafficking and torture, is detained after gun fight with authorities.
body: Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained by Mexican special forces on Friday
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.

Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.

Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.
A number of vehicles were pictured burning on a highway near Los Mochis, Sinaloa, after Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores was arrested
The two detainees were subsequently flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said.
When he was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.
Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the Beltrán Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.

His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.
Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground.
Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.

articles.title: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
articles.summary: In a statement to Italian media, his family remember him as "the greatest jeweller of our time".
body: Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.
His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.
Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.
The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".
The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.
Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.
The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.

"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media., external
"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.
"Thank you, Mr. Paolo, your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come."
Paolo Bulgari alongside David Bowie and his wife Iman in September 1991 in Versailles, France.
The post included a quote from Paolo Bulgari: "Everything can be a source of inspiration. There are no rules in creativity. Never."
The designer brand's celebrity clients have included Elizabeth Taylor, Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, Ingrid Bergman, Sophie Loren, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya and Rihanna.
Actor Zendaya wearing a Bvlgari necklace at the 2025 Golden Globe awards.
In 2011 the family sold its controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH, in a deal worth about 3.7 billion euros.
In 2019, he and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Rome.
The funeral will take place in Rome on Monday, 23 November in the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.

articles.title: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
articles.summary: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.
body: The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks. The BBC contacted the FBI for comment.

This comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.
It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US.
In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .
Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.
The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.title: Lock of former US President George Washington's hair sells for $4,000
articles.summary: The hair was given as a sign of friendship shortly before Washington's death in 1799, according to a descendent of its former owner.
body: George Washington died in 1799 after serving for two terms as America's first president
A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (£3,058).

The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.
Its new owner has not been named.

Saturday's sale is not the most expensive for Washington hair at auction. Three strands thought to have been removed from him close to or after his death stored in a locket sold for nearly $40,000 in 2021.

Gadsby, a resident of what in 1799 was the town of Alexandria in Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death later that year, according to a testament given in 1928 by Gadsby's granddaughter, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, and which was posted on the Richmond Auctions website.

McBlair stated that her grandfather came into possession of Washington's hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days" and had it framed and hung "under General Washington's portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life".
Gadsby hosted Washington's two birthday celebrations in 1798 and 1799, Richmond Auctions states.

Washington led American forces to victory against the British in the War of Independence and helped draft the US Constitution before becoming the country's first president in 1788. He stepped down in 1797 after serving two terms.
Several locks of Washington's hair have been preserved, including at least 50 examples that are in a collection at his former residence, Mount Vernon, which is now a museum.
"Public displays of hair from friends or loved ones peaked in the 19th century, but had long been popular among affluent families like the Washingtons," a blog on the Mount Vernon website states.
As well as lockets of his hair, other items associated with Washington have also done well at auction.
In July, a signed letter by Washington from 1776, in which he asks for soldiers for the Continental Army to fight the British, sold for $109,800.

articles.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.summary: Ukraine's president says Kyiv acted after 109 separate Russian aerial attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
body: Wes Streeting told Volodymyr Zelensky he was in Kyiv to show that Europe was united in its support for Ukraine

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.

A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimean Bridge
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".

Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".

Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."

Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.
Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.title: Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
articles.summary: The 30-year-old LA resident was convicted of arson leading to wildfires that killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings.
body: Homes along Los Angeles' Sunset Boulevard could be seen engulfed in flames during the fires of January 2025
A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.

Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu in January last year, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,800 buildings in the US state.
The conviction was handed down nearly five months after deadlocked jurors led to the judge declaring a mistrial.
Rinderknecht, who had pleaded not guilty, was convicted of two federal charges. He is due to be sentenced on 17 March when he faces between five and 20 years in prison on each charge.
Jonathan Rinderknecht's arrest in October last year
Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.
One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.

"We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.
Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.
Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.
Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".
"So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."
Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.
They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.
They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.
The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

articles.title: Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
articles.summary: Brussels sources had previously suggested the bloc might not apply the wider deal until fees were lowered for EU students in Britain.
body: Watch: Miliband says tuition fees for EU students are a 'separate issue'

A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.
The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a new youth mobility scheme.
However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.
Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband said "all the options will be on the table".
It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.
What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more
Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.
The prime minister said the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.
EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.
Miliband said it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.

"President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She said there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate issue, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.
Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary said: "Yes, absolutely."
"The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely."
Miliband said there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no new contributions to the EU budget.
He said previously announced agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".
Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".
He said that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively".
"Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.
She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the £17bn figure out of thin air, and said the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.
Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

articles.title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
articles.summary: The Russian embassy in Denmark has denied the allegation, which has led to Russia's defence attaché being expelled.
body: Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.
Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.
Russia's Embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.

In a statement posted on social media, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".
Russian state media cites the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".
Danish media named the target of the assassination attempt as the rapper known as Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.
PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.
Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said.
Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.

In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.

In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.
Russia's defence attaché must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.

He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Denmark is already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians can still get a Schenegen visa in another country and travel to Denmark. Denmark wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.
Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
Russia targets Kyiv crossings days after Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge

articles.title: French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
articles.summary: The court has upheld the 2020 beating of the black music producer as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
body: The three officers were seen on video beating up music producer Michel Zecler in his studio
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.

Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.
Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.
Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.
All were told they could never serve in the police again.

The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.
Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.

This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.
Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.
The case was heard by a panel of five judges.
The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.
They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.

After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.
The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.
During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.
In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".
Macron 'shame' at police beating of black man

articles.title: Anthropic shares fall after blockbuster opening as wider tech sell-off continues
articles.summary: Other tech companies have also taken a hit as share markets broadly slump.
body: Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off deepens.
The fall in tech stocks continued to weigh on markets, with the S&P 500 down more than 2% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 0.7% by lunchtime.
Both US indexes touched correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index also fell more than 3.4% by the middle of trading on Friday.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 12% to about $85 by lunchtime, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.
The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell.
Nvidia and SpaceX were both down more than 6%, while Tesla shares fell more than 3% and Meta was down 3.4%.
Apple, Amazon and Microsoft experienced smaller falls, while Alphabet was up by 1.2%.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - were also trading lower. Germany's Dax index fell 2% and the UK's FTSE 100 was down 0.5%.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.
Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?

articles.title: In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
articles.summary: A mathematician at Anthropic says he used an AI to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis, though verification will take some time.
body: Anthropic just went public with a major IPO this week
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 lines long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.
A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

articles.title: Germany taking seriously reports Russia may be planning to launch nuclear weapons in to space
articles.summary: Move would be breach of Outer Space Treaty and Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, which prohibit placing of nuclear weapons in orbit
body: The German government has said it is taking very seriously reports that Russia may be planning to launch a satellite armed with a ⁠nuclear weapon ⁠into ​space later this year.

The move – if confirmed – would be a breach of 1967 Outer Space Treaty of which Moscow is a signatory as well the 1963 Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty – which prohibit the placing of nuclear weapons in Earth’s orbit and test detonations in space.

The reports by a group of German media outlets reported, based on what they said were assessments by western intelligence agencies, come amid a recent rise in concern over the increasing militarisation of space which had the US Air Force secretary, Troy Meink, admit for the first time in September that Washington had deployed “on-orbit space control weapons”.

Germany’s Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) intelligence service and armed forces have exchanged ⁠intelligence showing that a Russian satellite, named Sputnik-S, ​was assembled several ‌years ago ‌and is stationed in the Moscow region, ‌a report by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung said.
According to the reports, warnings in early November said the satellite could be launched within 60 days and would be operational shortly afterwards.

“No, we haven’t seen ‌the report. But there are so many ‘alleged’ ​and ‘possible’ claims in it, attributed to who knows whom, that ⁠it’s certainly hardly worth ​taking ​them seriously,” Kremlin spokesperson ​Dmitry Peskov told ​reporters.

The Russian Embassy in Berlin said it was not aware of any such plans describing the reports as “unfounded allegations regarding the space activities of the Russian Federation” and calling them “part of a propaganda campaign”.
Moscow’s space measures, the embassy added, proceed “in accordance with international obligations” and serve “exclusively peaceful purposes”.

In 2024, Russia denied assertions by ​US officials that Moscow was developing a weapon that could destroy enemy satellites by setting off a nuclear explosion in ⁠space and triggering an electromagnetic pulse (EMP) to disable the electronic systems of nearby satellites.

US officials have alleged that Russia ​has ​for years been developing ​a nuclear weapon capable of ​destroying ‌entire satellite networks, ​such ​as SpaceX’s vast Starlink internet system that Ukrainian troops have been using.
Concern has been mounting in recent years in Europe and the US that Russia has been seeking to develop an anti-satellite weapon system which experts believe would probably employ an EMP wave.

Two years ago, Russian president Vladimir Putin denied the claim after then US president Joe Biden’s national security spokesperson John Kirby confirmed that the Russian Federation had been developing a “troubling” anti-satellite weapon.
“We’re not talking about a weapon that can be used to attack human beings or cause physical destruction here on Earth,” Kirby said.
Biden told reporters in 2024 that he believed Russia was developing the “capacity to launch a system into space that could theoretically do something that was damaging … my hope is it will not”.

While EMPs can occur naturally, it has long been understood that nuclear detonation has the ability to harm electronic systems, including energy networks, with both the US and Russia conducting high altitude tests in the early 1960s.

There has been increasing discussion over fears that Russia may be planning to place a nuclear weapon in space. Germany’s top military space commander earlier this year said he cannot rule out that Russia is working on technology to place a nuclear warhead in space, warning that such a move could cripple satellite services and make parts of the orbit unusable for decades.

“At the very top end of escalation, there is the suspicion that Russia may be working on technology to place a nuclear explosive device in orbit,” Maj Gen Michael Traut, commander of the German Space Command, said in an interview with Politico.

Asked whether he considered that realistic, Traut said: “I cannot rule it out.” He added that a nuclear detonation in space could impact up to a third of satellites in low Earth orbit with massive global consequences.

Suspicions over Russia’s ambitions to place weapons in space were given fresh scrutiny in 2022 with the launch of the Kosmos 2553 test satellite, which US and intelligence sources suggested could be a dummy run for the deployment of a nuclear weapon in space.

articles.title: Twenty Gaza students due to leave for Ireland after winning visa battle
articles.summary: Group’s evacuation follows campaign to overturn decision to deny visas to more than 60 students from territory
body: Twenty students from Gaza are to travel to Ireland to take up scholarships after winning a battle for visas that undercut the Irish government’s reputation as a champion of Palestinians.

The group is due to leave the territory on Monday under strict Israeli controls and travel via Jordan to Dublin to take up places at Irish universities. Another group is expected to follow next month.
The evacuation comes after a four-month campaign to overturn a decision by the Irish Department of Justice to deny visas to more than 60 students in Gaza who had been offered scholarships in Ireland.
The decision dismayed opposition politicians and other critics who accused the department of betraying Ireland’s record of solidarity with Palestinians.

The government backed down last week after a Dublin high court ordered the department to reconsider the decision. The minister for justice, Jim O’Callaghan, approved 48 visas. The first group is expected to arrive on Tuesday, with the remainder coming in late December.

“It’s a mix of feelings I still can’t fully describe,” Amir Alareer, 26, who is to study cybersecurity and artificial intelligence at University College Dublin, said via email on the eve of his departure from Gaza.

“There is hope and relief after months of waiting and fighting for this moment. But it is hard to feel complete joy when I am leaving my family behind in Gaza, and when 28 of my fellow students, who hold the same visas and share the same dreams, are still here waiting.”

The students originally expected to come in summer, and had supporting paperwork from Irish universities, but in July the Department of Justice rejected the visa applications. “The refusals hit us hard,” said Alareer.

The department demanded bank statements, proof of intention to return and other documents and said any appeal would have to be made by post, saying screening and verification were integral to the immigration system.

The students said such documents had not previously been requested and that Gaza’s banking and postal service had been destroyed. Ivana Bacik, a legislator and leader of the Labour party, accused the department of using “spurious reasons” amid a hardening of immigration policy.

Alareer helped to lead a campaign from Gaza that was backed in Ireland by demonstrators, a petition and an open letter signed by actors, writers and artists including Hozier, Nicola Coughlan and the rap group Kneecap. “Running a campaign from Gaza, through blackouts and displacement, was not easy, but I knew that if we stayed silent, our case would be forgotten,” said Alareer.

In October, the high court ruled that there were “significant and demonstrable errors” in the refusal of a visa to Shaymaa Abudalu, a 20-year-old who had been offered an engineering scholarship at University College Cork, and who was the lead case in a batch of similar lawsuits. A high court judge welcomed the decision last week to grant 48 visas and said “huge progress” had been made.
Among the students are five members of a dance troupe who have been offered places at the Irish World Academy of Music and Dance at the University of Limerick.

Alareer, who studied engineering at Al-Azhar University – Gaza, said Israel’s attacks on Gaza had destroyed his home and displaced the family several times. “The hardest experience of all was the famine, when we couldn’t find even a single kilo of flour.” Floods have impeded recent relief efforts.

His family was proud of his scholarship, he said, but saying goodbye would be hard. “They are happy that I finally have this opportunity, but leaving them behind after everything we have been through together is incredibly difficult.”

After studying software and innovation in Dublin, Alareer plans to return to Al-Azhar University and establish a cybersecurity department. “I want to build a generation of Palestinian engineers and researchers who can protect our digital future. Gaza will be rebuilt, and its systems must be rebuilt securely, by its own people.”

articles.title: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
articles.summary: Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship
body: Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.
Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.
“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.

Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.

In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”
Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.

The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge – a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic seaport of Kaliningrad.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.

At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.
Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.

Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.

More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, the Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli said in a statement it was alarmed by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.

There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”

Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.

In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.
Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer

articles.title: From mocked to mainstream: how Spain’s far-right Vox transformed its fortunes
articles.summary: Party that won just 0.2% of the vote in 2016 is on course for almost 20% this time and could be part of next government
body: Almost exactly eight years ago, a video clip of a stocky, bearded man riding a horse through western Andalucía went viral in Spain. The rider was Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, the soundtrack was a bombastic snatch of the Lord of the Rings score, and the caption was an equally unsubtle callback to the 700-year fight to wrest the Iberian peninsula from Islamic rule. “La Reconquista comenzará en tierras andaluzas,” it read – the reconquest will begin on Andalucían soil.

Celebrated by some, jeered by others – and inventively lampooned by those with sufficient skill and time on their hands – the video didn’t seem quite as amusing three weeks later when Vox broke through into the political mainstream by winning 12 seats in Andalucía’s regional parliament.

Until that moment, the prevailing wisdom had been that Spain’s experiences of the Franco dictatorship had inoculated the country against the far right, and that Vox was a tiny, fringe outfit whose prospects were terminally limited after it had picked up just 0.2% of the vote in the 2016 general election.

Fast-forward to late 2026 and the horseman seems less comical still. Vox, now the third largest party in Spain, is poised to pick up almost 20% of the vote in the snap general election on 29 November and, very possibly, to form a coalition government with the conservative People’s party (PP).

Abascal is going all out as the campaign enters its final days, peppering his patriotic appeals with familiar, baseless conspiracy theories. Last week he suggested that the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, was conspiring with dark forces to undermine democracy and change the country’s demographic makeup.
“The next elections may be the last that Spaniards get to decide,” he posted on X. “That’s what Sánchez and his accomplices at home and abroad are working toward … Vote so you don’t get replaced.”

How did Vox’s fortunes transform so massively and so quickly? The party was founded in late 2013 by disenchanted PP members who felt the conservatives had grown too indulgent of the demands of Basque and Catalan nationalist parties, but it struggled to make its mark. The highlight of its early years, during which it relied on hefty sum donated by the Iranian exile group the National Council of Resistance of Iran, was unfurling a large Spanish flag on the Rock of Gibraltar.

All that changed in the autumn of 2017 when a Catalan push for independence pitched Spain into crisis and left the PP government looking soft and ill-prepared. The crisis proved a godsend for Vox, simultaneously vindicating its distrust of Catalan and Basque nationalist parties and allowing it to position itself as an uncompromising defender of Spanish unity.

“Vox’s initial growth was driven by a reaction to Catalan nationalism – specifically, the sense around 2017 that Spain might fall apart,” says Miguel González, an El País journalist who covers Vox and the author of a new book, The Extremist Galaxy: Funders, Allies and Strategies of the New Far Right.
It gave Vox the profile it needed to pursue what González considers its most significant move: dragging immigration into mainstream politics and forcing a rattled PP to lurch further to the right.

“It was only an issue in a few specific places with high levels of immigration – such as El Ejido in Almería, or certain areas in Murcia,” González says. “[But] Vox has managed to put this issue on the political agenda, and, what’s more, the PP has gradually come to adopt some of their positions.”

This summer’s mass influx into Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta, when more than 80,000 men, women and children crossed over from Morocco, is a case in point. Abascal called it “an invasion and an act of war promoted by Morocco”, while the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo urged the expulsion of all who had entered, regardless of their age and individual circumstances.

The PP’s efforts to stop its voters slipping into the embrace of its far-right rival have led it into all sorts of contortions. Although Feijóo’s predecessor, Pablo Casado, famously rounded on Vox in 2020, accusing Abascal and co of peddling a politics based on “fear, anger, resentment and revenge”, the PP has repeatedly entered into regional coalition governments with Vox and now runs four of Spain’s autonomous regions with the party.
Related: Will Spain’s snap election in November bring a far-right party into government?

Vicente Valentim, a professor of political science at Spain’s IE University and the author of The Normalisation of the Radical Right, says that when centre-right parties adopt the language and postures of the far right, they end up legitimising it.

“After the initial normalisation moment when these parties first become successful – entering parliament etc – there’s a second step,” he says. “The centre right moves closer to them, starts speaking the same way that they do, starts going into coalitions.”

This can prove electorally expensive, he says. “The PP has moved closer to Vox, and when you have two parties that have such similar views on an issue as important as immigration, [some] voters simply prefer the original to the copy, and so they’re going to vote for Vox.”

Alongside a fixation on immigration, Vox has also brought its predilection for hate figures into the mainstream of Spanish politics – be they the secessionist former Catalan president Carles Puigdemont, the former leader of the leftwing Podemos Pablo Iglesias, or Sánchez.
“Vox talks about traitors and about criminals,” says González. “What Vox is doing isn’t offering political assessments, it’s making legal judgments.”

Abascal’s loathing of Sánchez is well documented – in 2023, the Vox leader said a day would come when the Spanish people would “want to see [Sánchez] strung up by his feet” – and his party’s manifesto vows to “undertake legal proceedings to have Sánchez and his government prosecuted for treason and crimes against the security of the state, based on their actions during the invasion of Ceuta”.
The party’s increasingly strident language has been matched by a more recent refusal to sever ties with some of the more extreme figures in its ranks and in its orbit.

In the run-up to the first of the two general elections in 2019, Vox was forced to drop the historian and commentator Fernando Paz from its list of candidates after Jewish groups complained about his “denialist and revisionist” approach to the Holocaust. Today he sits on the honorary board of the Foundation for the Defence of the Spanish Nation, a Vox-aligned platform of which Abascal is a co-founder and board member.

One pro-Israel lobbying group has expressed concerns in the past about Jordi de la Fuente, a Vox member and former neo-Nazi party leader who heads the Solidarity trade union, which was created by Vox. De la Fuente, who is awaiting trial for his alleged role in a violent attack on a centre housing unaccompanied migrant children in 2019, is standing as Vox’s candidate in Tarragona. Vox has insisted its candidate is innocent of a charge of “inciting hatred, hostility, violence or discrimination on the grounds of national origin”.

Alejandro Baer, a sociologist at the Spanish National Research Council who specialises in memory, genocide studies and contemporary Jewish studies, says: “A few years ago, the party was forced to distance itself from them, but now they don’t seem to represent a liability. Vox appears to be sufficiently consolidated and legitimate to openly incorporate people with backgrounds in these extremist spaces.”

Vox’s trajectory is plain to see in Rioja, a small town in the eastern Andalucían province of Almería. Long a socialist stronghold, Rioja was the only municipality where Vox finished first in May’s regional election – a poll that resulted in another PP-Vox coalition, after the conservatives lost their absolute majority. And yet the quiet town, whose palm trees and bougainvillaeas rustle in the warm November breeze, doesn’t exactly have the feel of a far-right frontier. Its divisions appear more generational than political.

Few of the younger people walking down the main road that bisects Rioja are surprised by Vox’s strong showing here. Fewer still appear bothered by Sánchez’s warning that a PP-Vox coalition will “roll back progress” and lead to the loss of hard-won social advances.

“My own ideology tends more to the right,” says Patricio López, 29, who works in an agricultural company. “I’ve noticed that people of my age tend to be more rightwing than leftwing, and I think that’s because they feel like they’ve been shortchanged. Housing, for example, is a much bigger issue for young people than it is for older people. And the left hasn’t looked after young people over the past eight years.”
One older resident, however, believes Vox’s surge in Rioja has more to do with protest votes from the young and the proximity of a large military camp than a rejection of its socialist past.

“I think it was just a gesture of distrust and revenge in the way Spanish politics is these days – it’s pure partisan theatre and it’s all very Game of Thrones,” says Rafael Ruiz Martínez, 63, who works for the local council. But he adds: “For those of us who lived through some of the Franco era, the Vox stuff doesn’t sound good.”
Another younger local man, who prefers not to give his name, agrees many people are sick of traditional politics and of a political class that has failed them.
“I reckon whoever gets in – whatever their political stripe – will do what others have done; they’ll dip into the till,” he says. “But politics is politics and people want a change.”

articles.title: Monday briefing: What could Andy Burnham’s reset mean for the UK?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: The UK’s intervention has reopened the debate over a future relationship with the EU, as the bloc faces the rise of the far right, a protectionist economic agenda and growing defence ambitions
body: Good morning. Nobody really wants to think about Brexit any more, save for the original Brexiters, who seem delighted that Andy Burnham’s “reset” with the EU has given them an excuse to get the old gang back together. But arguments about whether the UK should rejoin the EU will reignite in parliament this week, as Burnham briefs MPs on the deal he agreed on Friday.

That deal wasn’t so much a victory as the culmination of Keir Starmer’s incrementalist approach to UK-EU relations. Its core agreements haven’t been ratified by member states yet, and the EU won’t sign them off until Britain resolves a dispute over tuition fees for European students. Burnham is apparently “determined” to take the UK back into the EU, but don’t expect any progress on that before the next general election.

Putting aside the question of whether a second referendum would merely reopen old wounds, Europe has changed dramatically since 2016, creating new challenges for any government seeking a closer relationship with the EU. For this morning’s newsletter, I discussed these challenges and what they mean for rejoining with Mujtaba Rahman, managing director for Europe at the Eurasia Group and a frequent contributor to the Guardian’s Opinion section. That’s after the headlines.

Cop31 | The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal that “failed to meet the moment” in a dramatic finish to the UN talks in Turkey. The proposed deal failed to endorse a away from fossil fuels that more than 130 countries demanded.
Russia | A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.

Weapons| The Red Cross and other rights groups have warned that it will soon be too late to properly regulate the development of autonomous weapons. The warning came as the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded without an agreement on an instrument for regulating autonomous weapons.

UK news | Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal.

West Bank | Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot condemned arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank after dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday.

Three separate deals were announced at Friday’s summit in Brussels: one on food and drink, another on emissions trading, and a third on youth mobility, which will allow British students to work, live, study and travel in the EU and give reciprocal access to EU students in Britain (for a full recap, read Jennifer Rankin and Alexandra Topping’s explainer). Burnham wants to go further, and both he and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, have used the near-identical phrase that all options are “on the table” for Britain’s future relationship with the EU.

You’d be forgiven for feeling weary about revisiting the last decade in British politics. As one Labour MP recently told the Financial Times (£), “nobody is asking for this.” Burnham seems to be testing the ground ahead of a general election, hoping that a campaign to rejoin, or at least move closer to, the EU could plausibly win over progressive defectors.

Still, Friday’s agreement was a reminder of how difficult it is to negotiate with a club of 27. Member states, including France and Italy, issued a statement making it clear that the deal wouldn’t be implemented unless Burnham offered a deal on tuition fees for EU students at British universities. “There’s a fairly strong sense that we’ve reached the end of the incremental style of negotiating,” Mujtaba Rahman tells me. “There isn’t much more for the UK to do before it starts to resemble a cherrypicking state.” And there are other developments that will be on the minds of negotiators and ministers contemplating the UK’s future relationship with Europe.
Has the far right made the idea of European Union membership less attractive?

This is one of the major developments: Europe has become decidedly more right-wing since 2016. Though the European far right lost one of its key figureheads when Viktor Orbán was defeated in the Hungarian elections earlier this year, far-right parties govern in the Czech Republic and Italy, and support for them is rising in Austria and Germany. The proportion of voters in Europe who cast their ballots for far-right parties has grown more than five times since the 1990s, and has increased particularly sharply over the last three years.

Whether this will make rejoining less appealing depends largely on what happens next year in the French elections. Marine Le Pen, who is now favoured to win, wants to slash France’s contribution to the EU budget and drastically downsize the union. It’s possible that a Le Pen presidency could embolden other EU member states to seek closer ties with a pro-European British government, but it’s also possible that Le Pen’s domestic policies, such as reducing the retirement age to 60, could trigger a domestic economic crisis and inflame a conflict between the EU and France, one of its founding member states. “If Marine Le Pen wins, and France tries to enforce a domestic programme that runs in opposition to the EU, then I think a lot of people in the UK will look at the resulting crisis and think, ‘Thank God we’re out of that’,” Mujtaba says.
Is the EU’s new protectionism a reason to rejoin?

The EU’s Made in Europe strategy would have been almost unimaginable a decade ago, when progressives criticised the union for enforcing free-market globalisation on its members and forbidding state aid. The strategy, which uses public money to support goods made by companies in the single market, is a sign of both how isolated the UK has become and how much the world has changed. Burnham is now trying to make “reindustrialisation” part of his agenda at home, but the EU’s initiative is designed to disadvantage countries outside the EU. It risks scuppering his efforts by deindustrialising the UK car industry, which relies on European buyers.

“It’s very hard for the government to influence this because the Made in Europe negotiations are internal to the EU. And it’s very hard for member states to provide any guarantees because there’s no UK guardian at the table,” Mujtaba says. The EU hasn’t included the UK in the scheme, though Friday’s summit promised closer cooperation on steel and electric vehicle supply chains. But that may require the UK to follow EU policies without having any ability to shape them, making the idea of full membership much more appealing.
Would rejoining mean taking a different approach to defence?

This is perhaps the strongest reason of all for rejoining, but it’s also another area where the EU’s approach has evolved significantly over the last decade. “The geopolitical environment is forcing the EU to do a bunch of things the UK has historically taken issue with,” Mujtaba says. “It’s intervening in areas of policy that would have traditionally been the purview of nation states.” In particular, the EU’s Security Action for Europe facility (Safe), a new EU defence fund offering up to €150bn in loans to member states to fund defence investments, shifts defence from a national concern to one of wider European governance.

Britain refused to pay the financial contribution that Brussels wanted for it to participate in the Safe fund, though there are signs that the two sides may still reach a deal. But any campaign to rejoin would need to critically evaluate the deep ties and so-called “special relationship” between the UK and US in light of an EU that has grown to regard the US as an unreliable partner on security.

“The UK isn’t quite as far-reaching in its conclusions about the US,” Mujtaba says. “You don’t hear UK officials talking about the Americans in the same way that European officials are talking about the Americans.”

Sunday | Spain will hold snap parliamentary elections in what will be the country’s sixth general election in 11 years.

It was eye-opening to read about a British endurance swimmer’s three-day swim through the strait of Hormuz, in a quest to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war. Sundus Abdi, newsletters team

Football | Mauricio Pochettino argued Leny Yoro was wrongly sent off after suffering the joint-heaviest debut defeat in Manchester United’s history, losing 4-0 to Liverpool.
Football | Manchester City suffered a second successive WSL defeat, and a first home defeat under Andrée Jeglertz, losing 3-1 to Tottenham.

“Climate conference ends without final deal after rift over fossil fuels”, is the Guardian’s front page today, while Metro calls it “Complete Cop-out”.

The Mail has “Now five ex-PMs warn Burnham: Don’t rejoin EU”, and the Express writes “PM’s ‘empty words’ for sex abuse victims”. The Times says “Disability benefits could be tailored for each claim”, and the i Paper has “Universal credit set for major overhaul to help people into work”. The FT leads with “FTSE 100 giant Compass deals blow to London with move to New York listing”.
The Sun’s splash is “Paris: My Tyson’s schizophrenic”, while the Mirror has “My torment”.
David Byrne on the great ideas that got away

David Byrne, the frontman of Talking Heads and then as a solo artist, has made some of the greatest albums of all time. He tells Nosheen Iqbal about his new book Sleeping Beauties, in which he explores why so many breakthroughs in science, economics and culture were lost on their initial audience and only later revived and acknowledged to be great.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

David Parr’s days were spent decorating wealthy homes with William Morris’s much-loved textile designs. But by candlelight at night, Parr, a Victorian working-class labourer, would turn to the interiors of his own home, decorating his walls with his own beautiful designs, work that went largely unnoticed during his life.

After his death in 1927, those extraordinary walls in his home on Gwydir Street in Cambridge were thankfully preserved by his granddaughter, Elsie. Today, The David Parr House, as it is now known, is set to be honoured with a blue plaque, which is thought to be the first ever dedicated to a working-class Victorian art-workman.
